https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/06/ex-g.text: Former German intelligence chief August Hanning is accused of obtaining classified information from a former employee of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) and using it in connection with his private consultancy work.Germany's Federal Prosecutor's Office is reportedly investigating the 80-year-old former BND president on suspicion of offences including obtaining state secrets and treason-related espionage.Hanning allegedly continued to receive confidential documents from the intelligence service for years after leaving office. His former chief of staff is suspected of supplying him with the material and has also reportedly been arrested.According to reporting by the "Süddeutsche Zeitung", the documents included intelligence reports intended for the German Chancellery.Investigators are also examining whether classified information was passed on to foreign powers.The investigation reportedly emerged from information uncovered during proceedings linked to German businesswoman Christina Block and the alleged leaking of documents from the Chancellery.The allegations are based on joint reporting involving the "Süddeutsche Zeitung" and German public broadcasters WDR and NDR.

https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/actualitate/.text: Radu Oprea, ministrul Apărării, a anunţat că, luni, vor avea loc două misiuni de intervenţie asupra unor drone aeriene care plutesc în Marea Neagră. Una dintre acestea a fost semnalată în zona Sfântu Gheorghe, iar cea de-a doua la 45 de mile marine est de Mangalia. În ambele cazuri vor interveni echipe de scafandri specializaţi în neutralizarea dispozitivelor explozive. Cele două drone au fost semnalate de aeronava franceză Atlantique 2, care este dislocată în România în această perioadă. „Forţele Navale Române desfăşoară astăzi două misiuni de intervenţie asupra unor drone aeriene semnalate în derivă în Marea Neagră: o echipă de scafandri militari specializaţi în neutralizarea dispozitivelor explozive (EOD) se deplasează cu un dragor al Forţelor Navale Române pentru intervenţia asupra unei drone semnalate în zona Sfântu Gheorghe”, a transmis Radu Oprea, pe pagina sa de Facebook. Poti actualiza setarile modulelor coookie direct din browser sau de aici – e nevoie sa accepti cookie-urile social media El a adăugat că o a doua echipă de scafandri EOD evaluează pirotehnic elementele unei drone aflate la aproximativ 45 de mile marine est de Mangalia, iar intervenţia se desfăşoară de la bordul unei şalupe maritime a Gărzii de Coastă. „Cele două drone au fost semnalate de aeronava franceză ATLANTIQUE 2 , dislocată în România pentru executarea operaţiilor de descurajare sub egida NATO”, a subliniat ministrul Ap ărării . Oficialul a mai anunţat că Gruparea navală de combatere a minelor marine MCM BLACK SEA se deplasează din Varna către Constanţa, unde va rămâne până la 18 noiembrie, în cadrul eforturilor comune ale României, Bulgariei şi Turciei pentru menţinerea siguranţei navigaţiei. La cea de-a XIII-a activare a grupării MCM BLACK SEA, participă vânătorul de mine românesc M 271 „Căpitan Constantin Dumitrescu”, alături de nave ale Forţelor Navale din Bulgaria şi Turcia. „Misiunile grupării includ cercetarea, identificarea şi neutralizarea pericolelor pentru navigaţie, contribuind direct la securitatea maritimă a României în regiunea Mării Negre”, a mai afirmat ministrul Oprea. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw24.text: Figure caption, Watch: BBC reporter investigates deaths of family members in Russia-Ukraine war By Anastasiya Gribanova BBC Eye Investigations Published 25 November 2026 I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering. The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse. Image caption, The photo Anastasiya was sent of her grandparents' graves I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message. "Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said. It turned my world upside down. Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life. We stopped speaking. Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict. Image source, Gribanova family handout Image caption, Anastasiya (bottom left) with her father (top left) and grandparents (right) before the war Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located. After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV. Now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground , external . Image source, Ukraine's 33rd Mechanised Brigade Image caption, The remains of Anastasiya's family home are circled in a frame of a video, filmed by Ukraine's 33rd Mechanised Brigade on 27 January 2025 I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off. But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing dad just as much as I was. Image source, Aleksandra Gribanova Image caption, Anastasiya's father Serezha - he stayed in Dachne to look after his elderly parents I told her I wanted to make a documentary about dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet. I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals. Russia publicly announced the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since. This meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours. Image caption, Anastasiya could not safely travel back to Dachne, so she worked through contacts in village group chats In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call. Misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he said. It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time. "I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] said it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead. With the help of two other villagers, Misha said they had buried him in the greenhouse. "I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me. BBC Eye Investigations: Who Killed My Family? BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in Ukraine, uncovering painful accounts as she tries to reunite her divided family. Watch on iPlayer Listen on Sounds Watch on BBC iPlayer or listen on BBC Sounds now (UK only) If you are outside of the UK, listen to the Who Killed My Family podcast here Watch our YouTube documentary here , external As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated. Their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street. I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive. She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January. At this time, she said, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones." She said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians. "You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina said they had asked her. She said one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night. The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them. She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she said, despite the freezing conditions. With drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them. Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood. Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she said, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time. "If they had seen me they would have killed me too." Her theory was that my grandparents had irritated the troops in some way. "Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And [the soldiers] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me. Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence. The new local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, said she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing. These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified. The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia. The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear. Their bodies were not exhumed for nearly 20 months, when the local authorities sent them to a morgue in the occupied region, where a basic autopsy was carried out by a forensics expert. He told me that my grandmother had died of an explosives injury to the skull - but could not specify its cause. As for my grandfather, it said his body had shown no obvious signs of injury. I compared two satellite images of the house in which their bodies were found - from just before and just after when they are believed to have died - and could detect no significant damage to the building in the second image. I also spoke to a villager who said he had buried my grandparents. He said he did not know anything about who killed them. "I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked. Image source, Anastasiya Gribanova Image caption, Anastasiya does not know if she will ever be able to give her grandparents (pictured) a dignified burial I examined military maps from DeepStateMap.Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly. My colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me. I turned to the Ukrainian military. A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, said his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing. Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January. We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military. It said it had no verified evidence on how they died, or which implicated its servicemen during the "intense hostilities". It added that investigating allegations of wrongdoing was the role of law enforcement. We also approached Russia's ministry of defence and Russia's embassy in London for comment - they did not respond. Image caption, Sisters Sasha (right) and Anastasiya were reunited at Belgrade Airport The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske. However, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them. Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity. There is little more I can do for them, except one thing - mend my relationship with my sister and my mother. Almost three years after I last saw my sister, I fly to Belgrade where she now lives. Image caption, Anastasiya (left) and her sister Sasha look through photos of their father She is waiting for me at the airport, holding lilies, and a plate with a silly nickname on it that she gave me when we were children. We hug, cry and laugh. It feels as if something between us is finally falling back into place At her flat, we look through family photographs and talk about my investigation and what I was able to find. My grief is still there, but it hurts a little less. I'm no longer carrying it alone. "Are you ready?" Sasha asks. She rings our mother - who has also moved to Serbia - and puts the phone on speaker. "Hi, Mum. It's Nastya," I say. First there is silence. Then I hear her crying. "Nastya, my darling, hello," she replies.
